newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan rejects U.S. fears on N.Korea nuclear dump.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan rejects U.S. fears on N.Korea nuclear dump.

text.p: Taiwan vowed on Thursday to go ahead with a controversial plan to dump nuclear waste in communist North Korea, rejecting a U.S. call to consider other sites or store it at home.

The economics ministry said state utility Taiwan Power Co's contract to ship up to 200,000 barrels of low-radiation waste to Pyongyang followed strict international laws and posed no political or military threat.
"We can't see why we cannot ship the waste to North Korea since it does not pose any health hazard, nor is it illegal," a a ministry spokesman told Reuters by telephone.
Taipower told Reuters it was ready to begin shipping as soon as North Korea submits a final disposal plan.
"After that, we will get an export approval from the Atomic Energy Council," a Taipower executive said.

A U.S. official said on Wednesday that Washington had raised concerns with Taiwan over its plan to ship contaminated clothing, gloves and helmets discarded from Taiwan's three nuclear power plants to North Korea.
"We have raised with them environmental concerns, concerns over safety of shipping and storage," an acting assistant secretary of state, Charles Kartman, told Congress.
Kartman acknowledged that North Korea had a dire need for money and that cash-rich Taiwan, whose sole waste dump is nearly full, was willing to pay to dispose its waste overseas.
"We would like them to go elsewhere but nonetheless they have this need," Kartman said, adding that construction by Taiwan of its own dump was the "appropriate solution".
Taipower has declined to comment on press reports that it would pay Pyongyang US$1,150 per barrel to take the waste, which would make the deal worth up to US$230 million.
Taipower spokeswoman Huang Hui-yu said the plan was "definitely on" and did not conflict with U.S. interests.

"Basically, what the U.S. has suggested is in line with our own policies," she said. "We are seeking storage sites both at home and abroad. ...We are aiming to set up a new storage facility anywhere in Taiwan by 2002."
Taipower has offered US$116 million to any Taiwan community that agrees to establish a nuclear dump.
Taiwan is not an International Atomic Energy Agency member, but fully complies with its waste guidelines, officials said.

"Since the low-radiation waste has nothing to do with the nuclear profiferation issue, the agency said it would not get involved in this issue," said spokeswoman Huang. "Low-radiation material has no military or political value."
Since Taiwan signed the shipment contract with Stalinist North Korea in January, South Korea has sharply protested the move and sought international support to stop it.
